title: Blood groups & transfusion
examples: What happens if I receive the wrong blood type?
Why is the Rh factor important for transfusions?
Can I give my blood to someone with a different blood type?

explain.say: Today we are learning about blood groups and transfusions. You will learn about the ABO system first.

items: Blood cells: Red blood cells carry blood.
Antigens: These are markers on the surface.
Antibodies: These are proteins in the plasma.

explain.say: The ABO system looks at antigens on your red blood cells. You can have A antigens or B antigens. Some people have both A and B antigens.
Next we look at the Rh factor, which is a common test. The Rh factor tells us if the blood has the Rh antigen. If it does, it is positive.
Compatibility is very important when giving blood. You must match the donor's blood to the recipient's blood. Mixing wrong types can cause serious reactions.
For a real-life example, think about a blood bank. They must test every unit of blood carefully. This prevents dangerous reactions in patients.
A common mistake is assuming that all blood is the same. Remember, blood types are unique identifiers. Always check the type before transfusion.

faq.q: Why do I need to know my blood type?
faq.a: Knowing your blood type is crucial for safe blood transfusions. It ensures that the blood given matches your body's antigens.
asks: What is the purpose of blood typing?

faq.q: What does the Rh factor tell us?
faq.a: The Rh factor indicates the presence or absence of the Rh antigen on your red blood cells. It is tested as positive or negative.
asks: Is Rh positive the same as Rh negative?
How do I know if I am Rh positive?

faq.q: Can Type A blood give to Type B blood?
faq.a: No, Type A blood cannot safely give to Type B blood. This is because the recipient's plasma has antibodies that will attack the donor's antigens.
asks: What is the universal donor blood?
Is there a blood type that can give to everyone?

faq.q: What is the universal recipient blood type?
faq.a: The universal recipient is Type AB blood. This type has no antibodies that would react with most other blood types.
asks: Which blood type accepts all blood?
What blood type is the most compatible?

faq.q: What happens if I receive the wrong blood?
faq.a: Receiving the wrong blood can trigger an immune reaction. This can cause the antibodies in your blood to attack the antigens on the foreign blood cells.
asks: What are the dangers of mismatched blood?

facts: The ABO system is based on antigens on red blood cells.
Type O negative blood is considered the universal donor.
Type AB positive blood is considered the universal recipient.
Rh positive means the blood has the Rh antigen.

quiz.say: If a person has both A and B antigens, what is their blood type?
quiz.why: Type AB blood has both A and B antigens on its red blood cells, making it Type AB.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it only accounts for the B antigen, ignoring the A antigen.
wrong.1: This is wrong because Type O has no A or B antigens.
wrong.3: This is wrong because it only accounts for the A antigen, ignoring the B antigen.

quiz.say: A person with Rh negative blood can safely receive blood from:
quiz.why: To avoid reacting with the Rh antigen, the recipient must receive blood that is also Rh negative.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the Rh negative person's body will attack the Rh antigen in the positive blood.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the Rh factor must always be considered for safety.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the blood type compatibility must also be checked, not just the Rh factor.

quiz.say: Which blood type is the universal donor?
quiz.why: Type O negative blood lacks A, B, and Rh antigens, so it is least likely to cause a reaction.

wrong.1: This is wrong because it has multiple antigens that could cause reactions.
wrong.2: This is wrong because it still has A antigens that could react with some recipients.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the positive Rh factor can cause issues for Rh negative recipients.
